Photograph: BBC Queensland Child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as ‘safe’ day after she was admitted to hospital in coma Inquest into death of eight-year-old Queensland girl who was denied insulin by her religious parents told her case was complex Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Andrew Messenger Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as “safe” one day after she arrived at hospital in a coma and nearly died due to the neglect of her parents, a coroner’s court has heard. A Queensland coronial inquest heard evidence on Wednesday from one of the two child safety officers who ultimately decided to return the then six-year-old, who had type 1 diabetes, to the care of her parents at their home in Toowoomba. She died there on 7 January 2022 while her parents, Kerrie and Jason, and other members of their small religious sect prayed for her miraculous healing or resurrection. None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons. The child safety officer was given the duty of investigating Elizabeth’s home after she presented to Toowoomba hospital in a coma suffering from diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July 2019. He later became her case worker. Just one day later – after she was transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane – another child safety officer who assisted him completed an initial safety assessment of Elizabeth. She marked her “safe”. But her colleague told the court on Wednesday that Elizabeth should have been recorded as “unsafe” because they didn’t have enough information about her circumstances at the time. 5:49 Fourteen members of religious sect found guilty of killing eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs - video Elizabeth was later assessed as a child in need of protection, a legal standard under the child safety act. In 2021, both Jason and Kerrie were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to their daughter as a result of the 2019 incident, and Kerrie was jailed. The child safety officer later had a conversation with a doctor from the Queensland children’s hospital who told him Elizabeth was lucky not to have died and that Kerrie had not shown remorse as a result of the incident. The doctor said Kerrie continued to not believe in medicine and that it would be unsafe for her daughter to live with her until she changed her views, the inquest heard. “The pressure on dad around such strong religious beliefs will be difficult,” the doctor told him, according to his contemporaneous notes presented in court on Wednesday. “The team feel that the only way to force mum to see the concerns may be for Elizabeth to be out of home.” Elizabeth was sent home despite the objections of the Brisbane-based specialist paediatric doctors. The doctor told the court on Monday that she felt “stonewalled” by the officer after raising concerns about Elizabeth’s safety at home. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary arrangement that allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard. On Wednesday, the child safety officer said that the safety plan they adopted for Elizabeth “in hindsight, could have been more robust”. But he said he didn’t have a clear recollection of a meeting in which they discussed the idea of adopting the plan. “I do recall being in two minds about the best outcome for Elizabeth and her siblings, specifically Elizabeth being able to remain at home and connected with her family or out of home,” he said in a written statement provided to the court. He said it was a difficult decision and that there were practical considerations of how to manage the complex case. The child safety officer said it was significant that Jason had repeatedly committed to provide insulin for his daughter. Elizabeth required daily insulin injections to live. The inquest previously heard Jason, a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, subsequently provided medical attention for Elizabeth for two years. But he ceased doing so after being convinced to convert and then to stop treating her by the members of the group, and he stopped her insulin in late 2021, causing her death. All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens. The inquest continues. https://www.koreaherald.com/article/1089.text: Parliamentary speaker Cho discusses energy, defense cooperation with Croatian president Published : Oct. 10, 2026 - 12:39:25 Add The Korea Herald on Google Bookmark Event Link copied! National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik (left) poses for a photo with Croatian President Zoran Milanovic in Zagreb, Croatia, Saturday, in this photo provided by his office. National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik has held a series of meetings with Croatian President Zoran Milanovic, Parliament Speaker Gordan Jandrokovic and Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic to seek energy and defense cooperation between the two nations, his office said Saturday. In a meeting with the Croatian president in Zagreb on Friday (local time), Cho said the two countries have been maintaining friendly, cooperative relations since establishing diplomatic ties in 1992, which were upgraded to a comprehensive, future-oriented partnership in 2023. Cho has been on a four-nation trip to Italy, Vatican City, Croatia and Greece over nine days. National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik (left) poses for a photo with Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic in Zagreb, Croatia, Saturday, in this photo provided by his office. In a separate meeting with the Croatian prime minister, Cho also said the two countries should solidify their ties in the economy, culture, defense and energy sectors, highlighting a recent arms supply deal. Last month, South Korean defense firm Hanwha Aerospace signed a deal to export 18 Chunmoo multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS) to Croatia in an arms contract worth some 640 billion won (US$477 million), marking the first major arms deal between the two countries, opening up avenues for greater partnership beyond arms exports, such as industrial cooperation and military logistics support. Croatia has become the fourth European country to acquire the Chunmoo system, following Poland, Estonia and Norway. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/20/germ.text: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Azerbaijan and Armenia as Germany steps up its engagement in the South Caucasus, as the region emerges from decades of conflict between the two former enemies, who are now looking forward together to a future of peace.Wadephul said Germany sees the South Caucasus as “a region of opportunities,” adding that for Berlin it is important to establish “close relations” with Azerbaijan as Germany seeks to leverage “opportunities of connectivity, trade and education in the South Caucuses in our joint strategic agenda.” “Amid Russia's aggression against Ukraine and the economic situation in Europe, we are seeking new opportunities to find reliable partners for diversification. Azerbaijan is one of these reliable partners," Wadephul said.The EU has been engaging intensively with the region, as the prospect of open borders and improved regional connections could create new opportunities for businesses, facilitate trade, and strengthen alternative routes linking European and Asian markets. With the South Caucasus’ geographical position linking Europe and Asia, and with the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz disrupting global supply, the region has become increasingly important for global connectivity, international trade, and energy security.The German foreign minister said that the Middle Corridor global connectivity project linking Asia and Europe through the South Caucasus and Central Asia is “of strategic importance to Europe both economically and politically,” particularly “during this period of destabilisation".The Middle Corridor, a global transport network connecting China and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, has attracted growing European interest as governments and businesses seek to diversify supply chains. Wadephul said moving the Middle Corridor project forward had become a priority and that he would hold discussions in Armenia.The economic benefits of regional connectivity depend on regional political stability, reliable cross-border arrangements, and cooperation between neighbouring countries. For Berlin, supporting a stable South Caucasus is both a diplomatic objective and part of a broader European strategic interest. Wadephul told reporters that it was “important to move forward primarily through negotiations and dialogue ... amid tensions throughout the region."“Ensuring security and stability in the region is among Germany's main priorities," he said, adding that he "would very much like the peace agreement between Azerbaijan and Armenia to finally be signed and enter into force.”During a meeting with his German counterpart, Azerbaijan’s Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov acknowledged that without cooperation with Armenia, implementing the 42-kilometre Middle Corridor transport route, which runs through Armenian territory, might be difficult. Bayramov explained that the "entry and exit points of this corridor are the Armenia–Azerbaijan border” and “because of this connection with Azerbaijan's, (if) communications does not take place, then it simply has no meaning, no logic.” Germany's foreign minister also met Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev, whom Wadephul said was a "reliable partner".According to Azerbaijan’s official trade statistics, bilateral trade reached approximately $1.4 billion in 2025, with German exports including vehicles, machinery and pharmaceuticals, while Azerbaijani exports were dominated by crude oil. During his time in Baku, Germany’s foreign minister visited the Baku Synagogue to meet representatives of the Muslim, Christian and Jewish communities, given Azerbaijan’s tradition of religious coexistence.

https://bdnews24.com/world/europe/5jfcsi.text: Europe Poland in shock after six die in Krakow mass shooting Man opens fire in Krakow's main square, police say, adding the alleged attacker is a Polish Police officers stand guard at the site of a shooting near the main market square of Krakow, Poland, Nov 7, 2026. REUTERS bdnews24.com News Service Published : 08 Nov 2026, 09:24 AM Updated : 08 Nov 2026, 09:24 AM A Polish gunman likely influenced by far-right ideology killed six people in the main square of the southern city of Krakow before police shot and arrested him, officials said on Saturday, adding that three more bodies were found in his home. The scenes of blood and bodies strewn across the historic heart of one of Poland's main tourist attractions shocked a nation that has long viewed itself as safer than western European neighbours that have witnessed such attacks in the past. The mass shooting of unprecedented scale adds to the sense of unease built by a string of school stabbings in October which authorities said was influenced by violent and extremist content online. "Everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation," Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski told a news briefing. "Police officers are on-site, as are agents from the Internal Security Agency, both here at the scene and at the individual's family home." Polish authorities have said four women and two men were killed in the attack in the city centre. Seventeen others, including two police officers and the assailant, were wounded. Police said one of the dead people identified so far was a British citizen. An interior ministry spokesperson said that the five foreign nationals injured in the shooting came from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain. A spokesperson for the Lesser Poland Voivodeship office, the southern region where Krakow lies, told Reuters shortly after midnight local time that the injured police officers were in stable condition after undergoing surgery, and the justice minister called for blood donations for one of the wounded officers. The spokesman also said the shooter was in "stable but very critical condition" after multiple surgeries. Videos posted online had shown the assailant falling to the ground during a close-range shootout with police officers firing handguns. Bodies Found At Gunman’s House Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the bodies of two women and one man had been found at the shooter's home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, just under 200 kilometres north of Krakow. "There are strong indications that they are members of his immediate family," Tusk told a crisis meeting. He said a drone had been used to look inside the gunman's home due to potential security threats. "We know that a significant amount of weaponry may be inside the house," he said. Local media in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski reported that residents had been evacuated from the building where the gunman lived and that counterterrorism officers had entered the building. Speaking along with the prime minister, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating special services, said Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) are supporting the investigation. Military-Style Clothes Katarzyna Cislo, a local police spokesperson, said: "The shooter was wearing military-like clothes and used military weapons. Many ... weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle too." Police spokesperson Andrzej Fijolek told private broadcaster TVN 24 that the assailant used an AR-15 rifle and that he had a firearms licence. According to police, the alleged gunman was a 24-year-old Polish citizen. "The only known perpetrator of the incident is in police custody," they added in a post on X. They did not mention a motive for the shootings. Police said they started to receive reports at around 3pm (1400 GMT) that an assailant had opened fire from a car and had shot randomly at people in the square in Poland's second-largest city, a popular tourist destination. Unverified footage shared on social media showed people fleeing the scene as shots rang out and police sirens blared. Other video showed two people lying on blood-spattered paving stones and bystanders trying to resuscitate them. A third person lay motionless on the ground nearby. "I saw shots being fired from the driver's side window, and smoke was coming out. I ran to the police station in the main market square; when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor," a man who gave his name only as Konrad, and witnessed the shooting, told news website Interia. A 67-year-old man called Julek told Reuters that he saw a dark car appear suddenly before the driver started shooting at a group of people and drove off. "If we had been two minutes earlier, we might have been shot," he said. Unverified footage on social media showed shooting in the Main Market Square as traditional horse-drawn carriages, popular with tourists, passed through or were parked nearby. A man could be seen taking cover in one of the many restaurants and cafes that line the elegant square. National Mourning Kierwinski praised the heroism of officers who apprehended the suspect. "The police prevented a much larger massacre that could have otherwise occurred," he said. "They fired shots at the attacker just three minutes after receiving the report." A spokesperson for President Karol Nawrocki said he would declare a period of national mourning on Nov 8 and 9. "My thoughts are with the victims, those injured, and their families," Nawrocki wrote on X. Expressions of shock and condolence flooded in from around Europe. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the shooting "shocking." "On behalf of the Ukrainian people, and personally, I extend my sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims," he wrote on X. European foreign policy chief Kaja ⁠Kallas called it "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland."
